headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 0.53 (95% CI: 0.18–1.54), indicating no statistically significant association between calcium and renal cell carcinoma. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 85.07%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

sample_size.excerpt: Our study utilized a nested case-control study of the ATBC cohort including 154 RCC cases and 308 controls.
sample_size.location: Materials and Methods, paragraph 3; total_n derived from reported group counts 154 + 308 = 462

cases.excerpt: Among 154 newly diagnosed cases and 308 matched controls, RCC was associated with higher whole blood lead (OR=2.0, 95% CI:1.0,3.9; quartile 4 (Q4) v.

effect_size.excerpt: Results for whole blood lead were similar but the magnitude of association was more pronounced using only controls from the VDPP (Q4 v. Q1: OR=3.1, 95% CI: 1.1, 8.4), although the trend was not statistically significant (p-trend=0.300).

p_value.excerpt: Higher total serum calcium (P trend =<0.001) was associated with reduced RCC risk.
